- Taking a patron besides Allah is a refusal to use the will a person was created with.

15.text:
"Say, 'I truly fear—if I were to disobey my Lord—the torment of a tremendous Day.'" This is the penalty for the contravention of the order in verse 14, and it is put in a manner meant to win the heart rather than to threaten it. The Prophet ﷺ is told to say that if he himself disobeyed, he would fear the torment of a tremendous Day, which is the Day of Resurrection. The noble Messenger is protected by Allah from every sin, so disobedience from him is not a possibility at all. What the hypothetical does is teach the ummah how serious the matter is: if contravening a divine command is not excusable even for the greatest of the prophets, then who else can claim to be excused?

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, 'I truly fear'"** means: I know, and I am afraid. **"if I were to disobey my Lord"** means to rebel against Him, to worship anything other than Him, which would be a return to the religion they are asking him to accept, or to leave out what He has ordered, faith and good deeds being the first of them. **"the torment of a tremendous Day"** is what he would face then, and the Day is the Day of Rising.

### How serious the command is

The verses just before this one told them to keep away from shirk and to believe in the perfect power of Allah, Jalla Shaʾnuhu, mighty and exalted is He, and this verse names what happens if that is contravened. The threat is stated as a fear, in the first person, and the point of that manner is gentleness rather than force.

### The Day named twice

The wording leaves two readings of the fear. I would face a tremendous torment on an awful Day. Or simply: I would face torment on an awful Day. Either way, the point of putting it this way is that the person who is the closest to Allah is the one who fears most, and the community is meant to read the sentence as being about them. The fear of the Day of Qiyamah is what keeps the shirk out of a life, and the same Day that verse 12 promised mercy for is the Day this verse trembles at.

### In short

- The verse states the consequence of going against the command in verse 14: the torment of a tremendous Day.
- The Prophet ﷺ is sinless by Allah's protection, so the "if" is a teaching device, not a confession.
- The lesson is the seriousness of disobedience itself, measured by the fact that even the greatest prophet would not be excused.
- Fear of the Resurrection and hope of the mercy promised earlier belong in the same mouth, in the same passage.

16.text:
"Whoever is spared the torment of that Day will have certainly been shown Allah's mercy. And that is the absolute triumph." One verse does the whole arithmetic of hope. The torment is turned away, and turning it away is mercy, and mercy is victory. The punishment of the Day of Gathering, al-Maḥshar, is described as horrendous and harsh beyond description, so whoever finds it lifted off himself should know that it was a great mercy from Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whoever is spared the torment of that Day"** is read two ways. It can be passive: the torment is turned away from him on the Day of Judgement. Or it can be active, with Allah as the doer: He turns the torment away. The word for the torment itself is left out of the Arabic in one of the readings, and understood. **"will have certainly been shown Allah's mercy"** means Allah will have been merciful to him, preserved him and forgiven him.

**"And that is the absolute triumph"** is that forgiveness, and it is called a plain, evident, manifest success. The word used for it, fawz, means being admitted into al-Jannah, Paradise, which tells you that deliverance from the punishment and entry into the Garden are one event and not two.

### What success is worth

The same claim is stated in another verse as its explanation: whoever is moved away from the Fire and let into Paradise has certainly succeeded (3:185). Success in this verse means profit gained and loss avoided, and no other victory can be compared with it. On the Day when God's scale of justice is working, the ones who succeed are those who went looking for the support that is real and made the true faith the religion of their whole life. The person from whom Allah keeps the punishment away has attained success through His mercy, and that safety is a clear win.

### In short

- Being spared is itself the proof of mercy, since nothing else could have turned that torment away.
- The verse can be read either as the torment being averted or as Allah averting it, and both readings say the same thing about who saves.
- Triumph means Paradise, so escape from punishment and entry into the Garden are the same gift.
- The successful on that Day are the people who relied on what actually has power, and not on backing that turns out to have no value.

17.text:
"If Allah touches you with harm, none can undo it except Him. And if He touches you with a blessing, He is Most Capable of everything." This is an article of faith before it is a comfort. The verse says that Allah, in reality, is the one Master and Dispenser of gain and loss. No created being can truly bring the smallest benefit to anyone or cause the smallest harm. What people see passing between one person and another, a favour here, an injury there, is appearance. Looked at in the full flash of what is real, it is no more than a curtain that is about to vanish.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If Allah touches you with harm"** means hardship and poverty, an illness, a trial, a loss. **"none can undo it except Him"** means none can lift it off you. **"And if He touches you with a blessing"** means good fortune, wealth, health, plenty, **"He is Most Capable of everything"** means that as He is able to give these things, none can take them away, and He has power over all of it, including the touching and the lifting. The address is to every son of Adam. Nobody can keep Allah's grace back, and nothing can overpower Him or stop Him from giving whatever He chooses to give.

The same claim appears in another verse, quoted here as its parallel: whatever mercy Allah opens for people, there is no one to hold it back, and whatever He holds back, there is no one to send it after that (35:2). The Ṣaḥīḥ carries this prayer, which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would often say:

> "O Allah, there is no one to withhold what You have given, and no one to give what You have withheld, and the standing of a man of standing is of no use to him against You."

### What that belief did to people

This is one of the revolutionary beliefs of Islam. It taught Muslims to drop dependence on created things and rely on the Creator alone. Out of it came an unprecedented company of people who won hearts without trying: with meager means and constant hunger, they weighed more than a whole world, because they would not bow their heads before anyone. A Persian poet caught the same idea in a couplet about love, where the cause is obvious and the blame is still pushed onto something else:

> Musk on your hair is the work of your own tresses, yet your lovers find it convenient to blame the deer of China.

Alas, the commentary continues, in spite of this plain verse and the long teaching of the Prophet ﷺ, this ummah has gone off course in exactly this matter, handing out to created beings what belongs to Allah alone. Today a very large number of Muslims, instead of calling on Allah and asking Him in the hour of distress, cry out for help under all sorts of names, and the name of Allah does not seem to occur to them. To pray to Allah by way of the spiritual standing of prophets and of men of Allah is a different thing, and it is allowed, with evidence for it inside the Prophet's ﷺ own teaching. But to call directly on a created being, or to pray to one, to have a need met or a problem solved, is open rebellion against this command in the Qur'an.

### What the Prophet ﷺ told a young man

Under his comments on this verse, al-Baghawī reports from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās an hour on a ride. The Prophet ﷺ mounted, and asked the boy to sit behind him. After some distance he turned to him and said: young man. Here I am, he answered, at your service, O Messenger of Allah. Is there anything I can do? The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Remember Allah, and Allah will remember you. If you remember Allah you will find Him in front of you in every situation. Know Allah when you are at ease and comfortable, and He will know you when trouble comes. When you ask, ask only Allah. When you need help, seek help only from Allah. Whatever is going to happen in this world has already been written by the writer of destiny. If every created being were to combine to bring you a benefit for which Allah has kept no share, they would not be able to do it. And if they all came together to inflict a harm that is not in your lot, they would never be capable of it. If you are confident you can hold to patience, then do it by all means. If you do not have the strength for it, then still be patient, because there is great good and barakah in being patient with what goes against your temperament. And understand this clearly: the help of Allah comes with patience, ease comes with hardship, and prosperity comes with adversity."

The same hadith appears in at-Tirmidhī and in the Musnad of Aḥmad with sound chains of authority.

### Why no one else can act

The universe is not a heap of separate objects. Its parts are so connected that for anything at all to happen, the whole of it has to be coordinated together, and nobody controls that. Even the smallest event arrives only when countless factors in the universe come together to start it going, and God alone is the one who controls those factors. In the middle of all of them, a human being owns only a will. So blessings and afflictions alike happen by the direct orders of God, and a man who thinks he can rescue one person or finish another is talking like a fool. It is just as empty to live in fear of anybody except God, or to build your hopes on anyone but Him.

The inner reading goes one step further and takes that single origin seriously. Just as Allah is one and without partner in creating harm, He is one and without equal in pushing harm away. If everyone in the world gathered, jinn and mankind joining hands, to produce a pain that is not there, they would not manage it. And if they gathered to remove a pain that is there, without Allah willing it, they would find no way in. So know this: the wellspring of pain and of remedy is one. Blessing and trial come out of one place. Faith and unbelief rise from one place. Inside the circle of togetherness they all have one color, and only at the way stations of dispersion do they look multicolored. A poet of this way put the double face in verse: on your two cheeks sit both unbelief and faith, and on your two lips sit both pain and its cure.

### In short

- Real agency belongs to Allah alone: He removes harm and He gives blessing, and nobody can undo either.
- The belief is meant to wean people off dependence on created things, and it has a long history of producing unbowable heads.
- Asking Allah through the standing of His prophets and saints is one matter. Calling on a creature directly is another, and that is what the verse forbids.
- The hadith to Ibn ʿAbbās makes the same point practical: remember Allah in ease, ask Him alone, and accept what was never written for you.
- No event in the universe happens without its whole system agreeing, and that system has only one controller.

18.text:
"He reigns supreme over His creation. And He is the All-Wise, All-Aware." Verse 17 said that harm and blessing are in one hand. Verse 18 gives the reason: He is dominant over His servants, and wisdom and awareness go with that dominance. His mastery over them is absolute, and everyone stays under His power and control all the time.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He reigns supreme over His creation"** translates al-Qāhir, the Dominant, the Vanquisher, the Omnipotent, the All-Conquering. He is the Irresistible, above His servants, in the way that befits Him. To Him necks are bent, tyrants are humbled before Him, and He has complete control over everything. Nothing is impossible for Him, and nothing can overpower or defeat Him. The creatures bow before Allah and are small before His grace, his honor, his pride, his greatness, his highness and his ability over all things, because they all sit under his irresistible decision and power. He breaks the pleasures of His servants, and in essence and in attributes He is above all the travelers on the road.

**"And He is the All-Wise"** means wise in all He does, wise in His creation, wise in His command and decree, in His handling of matters and in the laws He sets. **"All-Aware"** means fully informed about everything: He places each thing where it belongs, and He gives favor and favors whoever deserves it. He knows people's innermost thoughts as well as their outward actions, and nothing about His creatures or their deeds is hidden from Him. He perceives what cannot be perceived, and He sees the unseen face to face.

### Why nobody gets everything they want

The two names at the end of verse 18 are doing a piece of work together. Al-Qāhir points to Allah's perfect power, and al-Ḥakīm to knowledge that leaves nothing out. Perfection in power and perfection in knowledge belong to Him and to nobody else, and that is why no human being, however great, comes out successful at everything he tries, or has every wish granted, whether he is a prophet close to Allah or the most powerful ruler on earth.

One of the great sayings of this path puts the same teaching as an exchange rate: one breath with the Real, in return for both worlds, is cheap. A hundred thousand spirits would be a fair price for one sight of Him, and it costs nothing. One moment of intimacy with Him is sweeter than the spirit itself. Anyone killed in this work is standing between fire and joy, and anyone who does not know this work is locked in the prison of his own mortal nature. And the prayer that belongs to it: Allah, seeing You is near, and at that nearness the work is too subtle for me. Allah, everyone is standing on something, and I do not know what I am standing on. I fear only the moment when what I am appears. Since the one who is in remembrance is happy with You, why should the one who is happy with You lament? When a person holds a sweetheart like You in his arms, how would he even notice the noise of the Resurrection?

### In short

- "Reigns supreme" means total dominance, with every creature's neck bent, and it arrives as the reason for what verse 17 claimed.
- "All-Wise" and "All-Aware" put power and knowledge together, and only Allah has both in full.
- Because His wisdom decides the outcome, no one, prophet or king, gets everything he tries for.
- The inner reading makes His being "above His servants" a rank rather than a place, and the traveler's only profit is one moment with Him.

19.text:
"Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, 'Who is the best witness?' Say, 'Allah is! He is a Witness between me and you. And this Quran has been revealed to me so that, with it, I may warn you and whoever it reaches.'" This verse answers a demand for credentials, and it answers it in a way that changes the question. Somebody had been asked to testify, and Allah offers Himself as the witness instead, then hands the same testimony to a Book that is still traveling. The clause "and whoever it reaches" extends the warning past the people standing in front of the Prophet ﷺ to everyone the Qur'an arrives at, and that single phrase is what makes the surah's argument a live case in every later generation, including this one.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, 'Who is the best witness?'"** was revealed out of an occasion reported widely. A deputation of the people of Makkah came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: you claim to be a Messenger of Allah, so who is your witness for that? We have not yet found a man to attest to its truth, and we tried hard to confirm it from the Jews and the Christians. On another telling of the demand it runs: produce for us someone to testify to the truth of your prophethood, since the People of the Scripture have denied you. The question, then, is: what thing carries the most weight in testimony, and what is fairer and more pleasing as evidence?

**"Say, 'Allah is!'"** Say it even if they will not. There is no other answer available, and no witness more truthful than the Real's own testimony to what He testified at the very first. He is the witness between us that I am His Messenger and that this Qur'an is His speech. He knows what I brought to you and how you are answering me, and the proof He gave is the miracles and signs He made appear to confirm the truth of this Prophet's ﷺ claim. "God bears witness that there is no god but He" (3:18) is the verse this testimony rests on. His is the witness that the Real is the Real, given on the first day at the covenant that has no beginning, with words that are true and speech that is pure, reporting a single existence, a self-sufficient being, majesty without end, beauty that lasts, an essence that never breaks off, and attributes that stand on their own.

**"And this Quran has been revealed to me so that, with it, I may warn you and whoever it reaches"** widens the audience to everybody, human or jinn, that the Qur'an arrives at. Gabriel brought this Book down to him, and the Qur'an is inspired to the Prophet ﷺ so that he may make people fear. Whoever it reaches has a warner, whoever it reaches has been warned. The same point comes out in another hadith: to whoever the Qur'an reaches, I am his warner. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr put it in a sentence of his own: whoever the Qur'an has reached is like someone who visited Muḥammad ﷺ in person. Because the warning travels by the Book and not by the man, the Prophet ﷺ pressed his Companions hard to pass on what they had, telling people what he told them even if it was one verse. And ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd reports him saying: may Allah keep hale and hearty a person who heard a saying of mine, kept it in memory and then delivered it to my ummah. That matters, because a man may not himself grasp the sense of what he has heard, while someone in a later time, who got it from him, understands it far better.

The obligation of this verse, then, falls on the ummah as well as on the individuals in it, and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas drew the duty from it plainly: whoever follows the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ought to call people to what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called them to, and to warn them against what he warned them against. Since the Book reaches people everywhere, those of the sects that refuse it have the Fire as the place they are promised (11:17).

**"Do you ˹pagans˺ testify that there are other gods besides Allah? Say, 'I will never testify ˹to this˺!'"** The question is not really a question. It is a disavowal. Do you, O people of Makkah, in sober fact bear witness that there are gods besides Allah, meaning the idols, which you call the daughters of Allah? And if they do testify, do not testify along with them (6:150). I bear no such witness with you, and what you acknowledge is false. **"And say, 'There is only One God. And I totally reject whatever ˹idols˺ you associate with Him.'"** He is one God, the only one worthy of worship, with no partner, no sharer and no associate in His unspoiled divinity, and I am innocent of what you set up beside Him.

### Why the Book is the arbiter

In the standing quarrel between the people of the truth and the people of falsehood, the one factor that decides is the Book of God. Nobody knows the full facts, and nobody has real authority, except God. So God, who is the only Being able to end the dispute, gave the parties an arbiter, and that arbiter is the Qur'an. That leaves one course. A person who is not sure the Qur'an is true should investigate until he is satisfied that it is God's Book. Once he knows that, he has to accept whatever it settles, and the man who will not agree with its decision runs the risk of being forced onto its verdict in the Hereafter, after degradation and punishment. The Book was revealed so that people learn, before the time of judgement arrives, what is waiting for them, and it tells in advance how God will treat people in the world that lasts. Whoever is given the job of delivering the message is clear of the responsibility once he has conveyed it fully, and whoever receives it is clear in God's eyes only when he accepts it and changes accordingly. The preacher's part ends at preaching. The hearer's part ends at doing what the religion asks.

The same verse has been read as a lesson in how to testify at all. Abū ʿAbdallāh al-Qurashī read it as Allah teaching His servants, and as a straight lead for seekers. In His own gentleness Allah is teaching the servants how to bear witness, in their measure, to His oneness and His being alone, the way He bears witness about Himself in a way that befits Him. Leave off the Ṭarīqah of resistance, the path of pushing back, or you will fall into the pit like Iblīs, abandoned. Others said about this that Allah bears witness to His oneness, His being one and His self-sufficiency, while everyone else, the angels and the people of knowledge among them, bears witness by agreeing that what Allah testified about Himself is true. He Himself testified to His lordship, His greatness and His oneness, because nobody else was fit to testify for Him. Created beings cannot reach the inmost core of His majesty and His tremendousness, and all their witnessing amounts to is agreeing that His witnessing is true.

Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, Abū ʿAbdallāh, said that people's witnessing stands on four pillars: following the commands, keeping away from what is prohibited, being content, and approving. It is also said that witnessing comes in three kinds. The witnessing of ordinary people is coming out of associationism, the tawḥīd of partners. The witnessing of the elect is entering into contemplation. The witnessing of the elect of the elect is a breeze of companionship blowing from the direction of nearness, for the sake of union. Someone who purifies himself sees everything as coming from Him. Someone who knows Him sees everything in Him. Someone who voices tawḥīd sees everything as He. Every being that has a name is a loan. Real existence is His, and the rest are under suspicion. Say "Allah", and then leave them (6:91). All is He, and that is the end of it, so how could anyone appear alongside Him?

### In short

- The demand for a witness was answered with the greatest possible one, and the testimony cited for it is Allah's own, in 3:18.
- "Whoever it reaches" makes the Qur'an itself the warner for every generation after, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said that reaching the Book is like meeting the Prophet ﷺ.
- Conveying one verse counts, and the messenger's duty ends with delivery while the hearer's ends with obedience.
- To testify that other gods exist is a claim the Prophet ﷺ refuses to join, and the surah tells him not to testify with those who do.
- In a dispute nobody except God knows the whole facts, which is why the Book is the arbiter, and refusing its ruling has a cost that is paid in the next world.

20.text:
"Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize him ˹to be a true prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Those who have ruined themselves will never believe." The people who said they had asked the Jews and the Christians and found nobody to testify are answered here, and the answer is that they knew. Recognition is not the shortage. What is short is the willingness to pay for it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those to whom We gave the Scripture"** means the holders of the Torah among the Jews and the Gospel among the Christians, and the knowledge written in them. They know what he brought them, Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā, the way a man knows his own son, because they had good news of him from the earlier Messengers and prophets: his coming, his qualities, the land he would be born in, his migration, and what his community would be like. The Torah and the Injil carry a full description of his physical features, his home city, and the place he would live in after the migration, along with his habits, his morals and what he would achieve, in such detail that a person could not fail to identify him. And the two scriptures do not stop with him: they carry a detailed account of his noble Companions as well. So nobody who recited the Torah and the Injil and believed in them could possibly miss recognizing him.

**"as they recognize their own children"** chooses the direction of the simile deliberately. It does not say: as children recognize their parents. A parent's recognition of a child is the most detailed and certain kind there is. The child is in front of them day and night, in every condition, raised in their hands and on their laps from infancy into boyhood. Children cannot know their parents to that degree.

One question about this simile was put to ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām, who had belonged to the Jewish faith and then became a Muslim, and it was put to him by Farūq al-Aʿẓam: Allah says in the Qur'an that you recognize our Messenger the way you recognize your sons. Why? His answer went further than the comparison. We know the Prophet ﷺ from the qualities and the features Allah made known through the Torah, he said, so our knowledge of him is certain and absolute. Our own children are not like that, because a person could doubt whether a child is really his.

**"Those who have ruined themselves will never believe"** are the people who lost their own souls by walking into the fire of Hell, and they will not believe in him. Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and his followers are named as the ones who ruined their own souls in this way, by losing this world and the next. Theirs is the final loss: they ruin themselves at their own hands, losing this world and the next together, and they refuse to believe in a matter so clear, a matter the earlier prophets announced and that was spoken of in former times and in these.

### Why recognition did not turn into faith

Reality is not foreign to a person. It is part of his own make-up, and it speaks one silent language through the whole universe. For the Jews and the Christians recognition was even plainer, because their prophets and their books had announced the last of the prophets and this Qur'an so clearly that knowing him was like knowing their sons. So why not accept? Because of the fear of a loss right now. Accepting the truth costs a person his high standing: he has to come down from it, step outside the crowd he belongs to, and give up advantages that came ready-made. When a man will not pay that, he refuses the truth, and for a gain he can hold today he pushes himself into a loss that lasts.

### Zayd ibn Saʿnah's test

Zayd ibn Saʿnah, who had been one of the People of the Book, recognized the Prophet ﷺ from the description of his qualities and features in the Torah and the Injil. One quality alone could not be confirmed from what came earlier, so he decided to test it: his forbearance would get the better of his anger. He went to see him, put him to that test, and found him true to it, and he became a Muslim on the spot.

### In short

- Recognition was complete, and it is compared to the surest knowledge a person has, a parent's knowledge of a child.
- The Torah and the Gospel are said to carry his description, his city, his migration, his character, his community, and even his Companions.
- ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām said the knowledge they had was more certain than the knowledge of an offspring, since parentage can be doubted.
- What stops belief is not evidence but the price: status, conformity and ready-made advantage.
- Ruining yourself is losing both worlds by refusing what you already recognized.

21.text:
"Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His signs?" The question is rhetorical, and the answer is: nobody. This is the worst thing a person can do, and the verse names two versions of it, inventing about Allah and rejecting what Allah sent. Then it states where either of them ends.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah"** means attributing to Him partners He never gave Him, saying that He has daughters, as the people of Makkah said of their idols, or claiming that Allah sent you when He did not. No one is more daring, and no one acts with greater wrongdoing, than the person who invents something about Allah and worships alongside Him what he invented. **"or deny His signs"** means refusing the proofs, the verses and the evidences He has shown, that is, the Qur'an and Muhammad ﷺ, which is the other way to do the same wrong. **"Indeed, the wrongdoers will never succeed"** covers both of them whoever invents the lie and whoever refuses the signs. Neither will ever get success, and neither will escape or be safe from Allah's torment. Those who do wrong by setting up partners and by denying His verses will not prosper, if they do not repent.

### The excuses keep working, until they stop

A man who has taken a stand is rarely short of reasons for it. In this world of trial he keeps finding explanations and justifications that support him, and words to wave away the arguments for the truth, until he feels free to twist it deliberately and announce that the real truth is whatever he has chosen. It works because he has put something other than God at the centre of his attention, and around anything at the centre of attention a magic halo slowly forms. He feeds himself on wishful thinking until he feels he has a grip on a support that cannot move. The people who did this are named in verse 20 as those who ruined their own souls, knowing and refusing.

### In short

- Fabricating about Allah and denying His signs are two halves of one wrong, and both are named here.
- The first is claiming a rank, a partner or a son that Allah did not claim for Himself. The second is rejecting the proofs that arrived.
- The excuses that make refusal comfortable are themselves part of the trial, and they are the reason such people are described as ruining themselves.
- Neither kind succeeds, and the only exit the verse leaves open is repentance.

22.text:
"˹Consider˺ the Day We will gather them all together then ask those who associated others ˹with Allah in worship˺, 'Where are those gods you used to claim?'" The surah has just said that the wrongdoers will not succeed. Now it shows the trial where that verdict is passed, and the question that will be put to the people of shirk. Nobody is left out of the gathering. Disbelievers and the things they set up for themselves as objects of worship are collected together, and then the question is asked: where are the partners you claimed, the ones you worshipped and expected to intercede for you? Where are the resolvers of your problems, and why do they not come to help you in the hour that tests you?

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹Consider˺ the Day We will gather them all together"** is the Day of Resurrection, and the command to "consider" it is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, as a warning to his people. Not one of them is left behind.

**"then ask those who associated others ˹with Allah in worship˺"** carries the answer to a small question of wording. The particle "then" between the gathering and the questioning signals delay. The interrogation does not begin the moment they are assembled. They will go on standing in that state of wonder and confusion for a long stretch of time, and the reckoning will start after that gap has passed.

**"Where are those gods you used to claim?"** is a rebuke, and it asks for the claimed partners to be produced. The same challenge is put in Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ: "And remember the Day when He will call to them and say: Where are My partners whom you used to claim?" (28:62).

### How long the waiting lasts

A hadith reports the Prophet ﷺ saying: what will happen to you when Allah gathers you on the plains of the Resurrection as arrows are gathered in their quiver, and you stay in that state for fifty thousand years? Another narration says that everyone will tarry in the dark that day for a thousand years, unable even to speak to one another. That version was reported by al-Ḥākim in his al-Mustadrak, and by al-Baihaqī. The same pair of numbers stands in two verses of the Qur'an. In Sūrat al-Maʿārij: a day whose measure is fifty thousand years (70:4). In Sūrat al-Ḥajj: a day in the reckoning of your Lord is like a thousand years of your counting (22:47). The difference is explained by the weight of it. That day will be long in proportion to how hard the pain is, and the levels of pain differ, so it looks like fifty thousand years to some people and like a thousand to others.

### Why the question is asked at all

Allah knows what they claimed and what they worshipped, and He knows how they will answer. The question is not for information. It is exposure: the people who handed the work of godhood to things that cannot answer are made to ask after them in front of everyone.

### In short

- The verse opens the scene of the great trial, with everyone gathered and the claimed partners conspicuously missing.
- "Then" marks a delay: long standing in confusion before the questioning and the reckoning begin.
- The delay is described in two lengths, a thousand years and fifty thousand, and the difference belongs to the severity each group feels.
- The challenge to produce the partners, asked here and in 28:62, is a rebuke rather than a request for news.

23.text:
"Their only argument will be: 'By Allah, our Lord! We were never polytheists.'" After the question in verse 22 comes the answer, and the answer is a lie sworn on Allah's own name. The verse calls their reply a fitnah, and that single word carries both things that are happening here. Their answer is itself a trial, an ordeal that testifies against them. And it is also infatuation: these people were devoted to idols and to self-made objects of worship, they even slaughtered sacrifices for them, and on this day all that devotion has nowhere left to go but denial.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Their only argument will be"** means that no plea is left to them, no answer and no excuse at all. The grammar of the sentence allows the word to be read either as their quarrelling or as their apology, and both senses come to the same thing: they will be driven to this.

**"By Allah, our Lord!"** is an oath taken by the great name of the very One they are denying before. "Our Lord" can be read as a description of Allah and as a direct address, and either way the shamelessness is the point. It was the most terrifying of days, the day of being paid back, with the awesome proofs of their Lord's power and authority standing around them, and still they had the nerve to lie to His face.

**"We were never polytheists"** is the denial of associationism and of disbelief itself, and the answer is given with a "then" in front of it, which shows that even this was produced after a long period of deliberation.

### Why they are allowed to lie

Most commentators take the reply for something the liars did not think about either before or after. It is the heat of the awe around them and the collapse of their own nerve, a state in which a person says things he does not mean. But if you look at how that Day is described generally, another sense appears. Allah gave them the freedom to speak as they used to speak in the mortal world, so that everyone present could see their full profile, and learn that these people did not stop at disbelief and polytheism but were unmatched as liars too, since they would not give up lying even on a day this horrifying. A hint of that lies in Sūrah al-Mujdalah: "the day they all swear to Him as they swear to you" (58:18). Just as they swore falsely in front of the believers, so they will not hesitate to swear falsely in front of the Lord of all the worlds.

Then, when they have sworn their way out of the shirk and the kufr, Allah in His absolute power has their mouths sealed with silence, and His order goes out to the limbs of their bodies: now speak, and testify to everything they did. That is when it emerges that their own hands and feet and eyes and ears had been a kind of secret service, planted with them all along, and they will tell, and tell everything. ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī gave the verse in ibn-Kathīr's account a harder sense: there is nothing left to protect them from the affliction that will be put on them. Sūrat Yā Sīn states it: "On that Day We put a seal on their mouths, and their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will testify to what they were earning" (36:65). And elsewhere: "they will not conceal anything from Allah" (4:42). Ibn ʿAbbās explained that verse this way: they will lie as much as they can, and swear falsely, but once their own hands and feet testify, they will have no nerve left to say anything wrong at all.

The wrongdoer is left free to make whatever statement he likes before the Judge of all judges, even a lie, just as he lied in mortal life, and nobody snatches that right off him. Allah tears the façade of the lie down with His own power, through the testimony of the man's own body parts, so no advocate is needed. This is why lying will not work after death. Think of an entrance examination. After death the first test a person sits is taken by the two angels, Munkar and Nakir. In the hadith, when they ask a kāfir who his Lord is and what his religion is, he says only: oh, I do not know. A true Muslim answers: Allah is my Lord, and Islam is my religion, and I accepted Your oneness. The kāfir's answer is the one he will not be able to improve on by talking his way out. Nobody will have any courage to lie in that earlier test, otherwise a disbeliever could have given the Muslim's answer. The reason is that the examiners there are angels who do not know the unseen and who cannot make hands and feet testify. If lying were an option there, the angels would simply act on the answer given, and the whole arrangement would come apart. The test of the Resurrection is different, because the questions and the answers pass before Allah Almighty, and no lie works there even if a person tries it.

### Who these people were

Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ and Māzhari report from some elders a description of which liars are meant. They are people who never openly declared some created thing to be God or God's deputy. In what they did, though, they assigned all the powers of godhood to created beings: they went to them with their needs, made offerings in their names, and asked them for sustenance, for health, for children and for everything they wanted. Such people did not think of themselves as associating partners with Allah, which is why on the Day of Resurrection they will swear that they never did. In the end Allah Almighty exposes their disgrace.

### Does Allah speak to them or not

A question is raised by the verse, because some passages of the Qur'an state that Allah will not speak to the wrongdoers and the sinners, while this verse plainly shows an address being made. Two answers are given. The address here is not one that honours them or accepts their prayers, and what is denied in those other verses is that kind of standing and acceptance. It is also said that the questioning on that Day may reach them through the angels, and that the verse which denies divine speech has an indirect address in view.

### In short

- Their defence is a false oath taken on the name of the One they are answering, and it is the last thing their own argument offers them.
- Fitnah names both the ordeal they are in and the infatuation they are now denying.
- The lie is permitted to stand on the record only so that limbs, and then silence, demolish it.
- The same freedom to lie does not exist in the trial of the grave, where the examiners cannot be answered by words alone.
- The liars exposed here are people who never called a creature God, and behaved as if they had.

24.text:
"See how they will lie about themselves and how those ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them." The Prophet ﷺ is told to look at it. The lie they tell on the Day of Judgement turns back on them, and the fabricated partners are simply gone when they are needed. On another reading the address is to the angels.

### Phrase by phrase

**"See how they will lie about themselves"** means that the curse of what they say falls on their own selves. They have written the punishment of their own lie onto themselves by telling it. **"and how those ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them"** means that what they used to coin has vanished, absent from before them, useless, and those they worshipped on the strength of a claim leave them to their plight. The word for fabrication here opens two readings. One takes it as the partners they invented in the mortal world, whose unreality was exposed on the Day of Resurrection. The other takes it as the false oath they swear on that Day, the fabrication that their own limbs then uncover. A further reading connects it instead with the story they used to tell about their objects of worship in this world, for example the claim that "we do not worship them in order to make them gods for us, but so that they may intercede for us with Allah and bring us closer to Him" (39:3). That fabrication, too, was exposed on the Day, because nobody interceded for them in their hour of trial and nobody got their punishment reduced one step.

### Are the idols there or not

The verse appears to say that at the time of this question and answer the false objects of worship will not be present. But the Qur'an also says: "gather those who did wrong and what they used to worship" (37:22), which sounds as though they will be there. The answer is that their absence, in the sense this verse gives, means only that they are unavailable, as partners, as sharers, or as intercessors. They will be present, and will be unable to help the people who backed them in any way whatsoever, and so there is no contradiction between the two verses. It is also possible that everything is gathered at one time and in one place first, and then separated, and the question asked after the separation.

### Why a lie cannot be given up

Verse 24 carries a warning about a habit. These people were given free speech on the Day of Judgement, and they used it to deny their shirk with a false oath. There is a hint in that, and the hint is that lying is an evil habit and never easy to shake off. The same mouths that swore falsely in front of the believers in this world could not stop themselves on the day that disgraced them in front of the whole creation. That is why lying is condemned hard in Qur'an and hadith, with serious warnings attached, and why liars are cursed at many places in the Book. The Prophet ﷺ said: stay away from lying, because a lie is the partner of sin, and a lie and a sin both go to Jahannam. Ibn Ḥibbān recorded that in his Ṣaḥīḥ. He was once asked which deed takes a person to Hell, and he said: a lie, and this is in the Musnad of Aḥmad. On the night of the Ascent into heaven, the Miʿrāj, the Prophet ﷺ saw a man whose mouth was being split open at the corners, which then closed and returned to how they were, and then were split open again, on and on, all through the Day of Qiyamah. He asked the Angel Jibrāʾīl al-Amīn who it was, and the answer came: he is a liar. In another narration in the Musnad of Aḥmad he said that a person does not become a complete Muslim until he abandons lying altogether, to the point that he does not lie even as a joke or for fun. Al-Baihaqī and others report, with sound authority, that the character of a Muslim may carry other faults, but not breach of trust and not lying. And a further hadith says that lying cuts a person's provision.

### In short

- The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to watch the lie collapse onto the heads of the liars.
- "What they used to coin" can mean the idols, the invented oath, or the excuse of intercession quoted from 39:3.
- The partners are present on that Day and absent where it counts, which settles the surface tension with 37:22.
- Lying is described as a habit that survives even the Day of Judgement, and it is condemned in the Qur'an, in hadith, and in the vision of the Ascent.
- A lie also costs a person his provision, which is a worldly penalty on top of the next one.

25.text:
"There are some of them who ˹pretend to˺ listen to your recitation ˹of the Quran˺, but We have cast veils over their hearts—leaving them unable to comprehend it—and deafness in their ears. Even if they were to see every sign, they still would not believe in them. The disbelievers would ˹even˺ come to argue with you, saying, 'This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but ancient fables!'" The scene moves back from the Day of Judgement to the court of the Prophet ﷺ, where some people sit and listen. The verse explains why the recitation does not reach them, and it insists that the fault is not in the evidence: signs of every kind could be produced and it would change nothing.

### Phrase by phrase

**"There are some of them who ˹pretend to˺ listen to your recitation"** means that they come to hear him recite, and the hearing does them no good. Those named in the reports include They include Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb and al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, an-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith and Umayyah ibn Khalaf, ʿUtbah and Shaybah the sons of Rabīʿah, and al-Ḥarth ibn ʿĀmir. Another account gives ʿUtbah and Shaybah sons of Rabīʿah, and Umayyah and Ubayy sons of Khalaf, and says that they listened to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he recited, and then asked an-Naḍr about it.

**"but We have cast veils over their hearts"** means covers put on the hearts so that they do not understand the Qur'an, and **"deafness in their ears"** means a heaviness in the ears that keeps them from hearing what would benefit them and from hearing truth and guidance with any willingness to take it in. This covering is the consequence of their own stubbornness and turning away.

**"Even if they were to see every sign, they still would not believe"** means they will not believe in any sign, proof, clear evidence or token they witness, because their comprehension is not sound and their judgment is not fair. The demand that every proof be produced was put by al-Ḥarth ibn ʿĀmir. The example of these people, elsewhere in the Qur'an, is a herd animal being shouted at, which hears nothing but the shouting and the calling (2:171). And: if Allah had known of any good in them, He would have made them listen (8:23).

**"The disbelievers would come to argue with you, saying, 'This is nothing but ancient fables!'"** means that when they come to dispute about what has been revealed in the Qur'an, and he informs them, they say: what Muḥammad brought us was taken from the books of the people before us, that is, copied. An-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith is named as the one who said it. The word for fables, asātīr, is the plural of ustūrah, a tale.

### The man who was asked what the Prophet was saying

Ibn ʿAbbās gave the exchange behind the verse. Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb and his companions came to listen, and they said to an-Naḍr: O Abū Quṭaylah, what is Muḥammad saying? He answered: by the One who has made this House, the Kaʿbah, His own, I do not know what he is saying. I only see his lips moving and muttering something. As for the content, it is old wives' tales about nations that came and went, the same sort of story I used to tell you. An-Naḍr talked a great deal about bygone nations, and the people of Makkah, Quraysh among them, would listen to what he told them. It was then that Allah revealed this verse. So the verdict "ancient fables" was the report of a man who had just admitted that he could not hear a word of what was being recited.

### How prejudice finishes the job

In this world of trial a person never lacks openings for pretexts, and he will find a justification for whatever suits him. Some people appear to listen to the Qur'an, but where there is prejudice from the outset, the truth lands on deaf ears and never touches the heart. They raise mental barriers, and those barriers leave them ignorant of their duties even after the duties have been explained to them in detail. No argument moves them, however plainly it is set out. Whatever religious question they allow past the barriers is admitted only so that it can be disputed. Their aim is not to hear and understand anything that would change how they act, and so the shirk stays untouched, so they never lay hold of the side of the question that matters. They are quick to twist a religious matter, and they hunt inside every moral question for facts they can misstate, so that they and their followers can feel they are on the right path.

### In short

- Listening is real and the benefit is nil, because the veils and the heaviness are put there by Allah as the consequence of their own refusal.
- The people named as listeners are leaders of Quraysh, and one of them reported that he could make out nothing except moving lips.
- Producing every sign would not help them, since their problem is comprehension and judgment, not evidence.
- "Ancient fables" is the accusation of the people who were themselves busy with old stories.
- Prejudice builds its own barriers and turns argument into a tool for resisting guidance.

26.text:
"They turn others away from the Prophet and distance themselves as well. They ruin none but themselves, yet they fail to perceive it." This verse sums up a double manoeuvre. They block other people from the Prophet ﷺ and from the Qur'an, and they stay away themselves, so they combine both evils: they get no benefit and they let nobody else get any. The harm they are doing lands on their own heads, and they do not notice.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They turn others away from the Prophet"** means discouraging people from following the truth, from believing in Muḥammad ﷺ and from obeying the Qur'an. **"and distance themselves as well"** means they themselves keep clear of him, and do not let themselves benefit the way they refuse to let others benefit. **"They ruin none but themselves"** means they destroy only themselves by this action, and its harm touches them alone, **"yet they fail to perceive it"** means the fact does not register with them at all. They also carry the same weight of sin as the people they are warning off.

### Who the verse is about

Early authorities such as ad-Daḥḥāk, Qatādah and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah took it about the common disbelievers of Makkah, who kept people away from listening to the Qur'an and following it while they stood off from it themselves. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reports the same from Ibn ʿAbbās: they obstruct people from believing in Muḥammad ﷺ. Much the same was relayed from Qatādah, Mujāhid and ad-Daḥḥāk and from several others, and al-Suddī agreed. The disbelievers of Quraysh, on this telling, used to avoid meeting the Prophet ﷺ and used to put people off coming to him.

A second reading takes the pronoun back to the Prophet ﷺ rather than to the Qur'an, and makes the verse about his respected uncle Abū Ṭālib, who stopped people from hurting his nephew and even supported him, but would not believe in the Qur'an or follow it. Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported to have held this, and it was the view of ʿAṭāʾ ibn Dīnār and of al-Qāsim ibn Mukhaymarah, reported through Saʿīd ibn Abī Hilāl, and another reading names Abū Ṭālib as the one who warned people off harming him while not believing in him himself. The report of al-Walībī from Ibn ʿAbbās goes the other way, back to the unbelievers of Makkah.

### The poetry of Abū Ṭālib

Muqātil set the verse in a scene. The Quraysh assembled at Abū Ṭālib's place, meaning to get at the Prophet ﷺ, and he went to his uncle to invite him to Islam. Abū Ṭālib said:

> By Allah, they will not reach you, for all their numbers,
> until I am laid in the ground and buried.
> So carry on with your business, unobstructed,
> and take the good news and a settled mind.
> You have brought a religion which is most certainly
> one of the best religions on the earth.
> Were it not for fear of blame and of insult,
> you would have found me a firm believer in it.

The lie will be uncovered that same Day, in the words quoted under verse 22: they will say that those partners have vanished from us, and that they never called on anything at all before Allah (40:73-74). That, on this account, is what was revealed about: they warn people off and stay off themselves. The harm of the arrangement returns to the one who set it up, though he does not see it.

### In short

- Keeping others away and staying away yourself is described as a single act of self-destruction with two hands.
- One reading names the leaders of Quraysh, who avoided the Prophet ﷺ and blocked people from him.
- Another reading names Abū Ṭālib, who defended him with his power and refused him with his belief.
- The verse's last clause is the sharpest one: they do not even perceive that the ruin they are building is for themselves.

27.text:
"If only you could see when they will be detained before the Fire!" The scene is the Day of Rising, and the ones held in it are the wrongdoers who denied the signs. They are stopped at the edge of the Fire and shown what is there: the chains, the restraints, the punishment, all of it with their own eyes, and all of it past anything they had pictured. Then the wish comes out of them, and it asks for one thing only, to be sent back.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If only you could see"** is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. Whatever the sentence leaves unsaid is understood: see it, and you will be looking at an awesome sight, a remarkable thing in their trouble. **"when they will be detained before the Fire"** means being brought there, exposed to it and shut up in it with no opening left. **"Oh! If only we could be sent back"** is the cry of people who have lost every other way out. They want the world given back so that they can act differently in it. **"we would never deny the signs of our Lord"** promises a change about the Scriptures and the messengers they had thrown aside. **"and we would ˹surely˺ be of the believers"** completes it, and the wish is to belong to the believers outwardly and inwardly, the way they belong.

The two verbs of that promise, nukadhdhibu and nakūna, are read in more than one way. One reading takes them as a fresh sentence, so that the verbs of denying and of being believers stand on their own. Another reads them as the answer drawn after the wish, and then the forms say something slightly different: on the first reading they say, in effect, we will not deny and we will be believers, and on the second they carry the hope itself, that we would not deny and would be believers. The point is not the grammar. The promise itself is worthless, and the next verse says why.

### Why the hereafter weighs so heavily

Three principles carry the rest of faith: the oneness of Allah, prophethood, and belief in the hereafter. Every other article of faith falls under one of them. They tell a human being what he is and what his life is for, and that knowledge turns a life around, because it shows him the straight path. Of the three, the hereafter has the widest effect in practice. Belief in a reckoning to come, with good rewarded and evil punished, aims every deed in one direction. That is why the subjects of the Qur'an move around these three, and why the verses here press on the reckoning, its rewards and punishments, and the true nature of this mortal world.

### In short

- The verse shows wrongdoers at the edge of the Fire, seeing with their own eyes what they had denied.
- Their only wish is to be sent back, with a promise to stop denying the signs and to join the believers.
- The address "if only you could see" leaves its answer to be understood, and the answer is a terrible sight.
- Belief in the reckoning is singled out because it channels every deed, next to oneness and prophethood.
- The promise they make will be refused, because it is forced out of them by what they now see.

28.text:
"But no! ˹They only say this˺ because the truth they used to hide will become all too clear to them." This verse tears the promise of verse 27 apart. The wish to go back is not faith arriving, it is pain speaking. What they now say about believing was never the real condition of their hearts, and the proof is that the condition has just become visible to everybody.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But no!"** is not a plain refusal of the words. It rejects the desire to believe that the wish behind those words carried. **"˹They only say this˺ because the truth they used to hide will become all too clear to them"** means that the disbelief, the denial and the rebellion they kept folded inside have now been uncovered. They tried to keep them hidden in this world and they tried to keep them hidden on that Day, and both attempts failed. What they used to conceal was the oath they swore in front of the believers in this life: by Allah their Lord, they were never people who joined others in worship with Him. That claim has now become evident for what it was, because their own limbs had already testified against them in the scene just before this verse. **"Even if they were to be sent back, they would certainly revert to what they were forbidden"** answers the wish directly. Grant them the return they beg for, and they will forget every resolution the second they are standing in the world again, and go back to the disbelief and the association of partners with Allah that they had been stopped from. **"Indeed they are liars"** closes it: the promise that they would believe if only they were returned is a lie.

### What kind of lie is it

The wording leaves the charge of lying open in three directions, and all three fit. It can mean that the promise would not come true, since a people who lie their way out of the Day would go on lying once they were back in the world. It can mean that the words do not come from a real intention at all, since they are buying time and trying to step out of the punishment they are watching while they still have no wish to do what they promise. And it can mean that they are lying about what they had hidden, since they used to swear by Allah that they were not idolaters.

On the reading that sits closest to the sequence of the verses, the whole exchange runs like this. Their All-Knowing, All-Aware Master knows what they would do if He gave them what they asked for, and so He refuses it. They are not asking to go back because they want faith, they are asking because they are frightened of the torment standing in front of them. Fear of punishment is not belief. Their disease was never a shortage of evidence. They did not relish the realities the prophets of Allah had brought them, they knew the prophets were true, and they raised dust to keep those realities unmanifest, out of chronic obstinacy or out of worldly greed. On that Day everything comes into the open. They see the power of Allah with their own eyes, they know the truth of what was claimed, and the life after death they had denied is before them, real and physical. They are direct witnesses to reward, to punishment and to the Fire, and no argument is left to them. Their wish to be returned is then nothing but the absence of a choice.

### The Day that sorts out reputations

One reading takes this unveiling further, to the Day when states are uncovered and secrets brought out, the day when hidden cores are tested (86:9). On it many who were counted among the renunciants in this world, who wore the color of the close friends of Allah and dressed in their dress, will find the burning mark of wretchedness on their own foreheads as they are taken down to the dwelling place of strangers. And many whom everyone knew as shameless, whom they expected to see in chains, who owned nothing and had no name at all, will be the ones in whose name the treasuries of the unseen and the robes of generosity are carried in. The holy ones of the Higher Plenum and the dwellers of the Gardens of Shelter will stand astonished at what He does, and it will be as a poet said of the reversal: many a praying master of the path left without a mount, and many a tavern haunter riding off on a roaring lion. The same reading then adds that the people of punishment, if they were sent back to this world, would return to their refusal and denial, and the people of clear loyalty, if they were sent back, would return to the beauty of their deeds. Each of them goes back to what he already is.

### In short

- Their wish to return is forced by the torment in front of them, not by belief.
- The truth they hid has become clear, and their old oath of innocence is exposed as a lie.
- Sent back, they would revert to the disbelief and the shirk they were forbidden, so the promise proves false three ways over.
- They were never short of evidence. Obstinacy and greed kept the truth unmanifest.
- That Day uncovers hearts, tests secret cores (86:9) and reverses the reputations people built for themselves.

29.text:
"They insisted, 'There is nothing beyond this worldly life and we will never be resurrected.'" This is the sentence that explains everything before it. It is not a report about the Fire. It is the creed that put them there, and it is what they would say again if they were returned, which is exactly what verse 28 promised.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They insisted"** carries the sense of going back to something and sticking to it, and the wording ties this verse to the "they would certainly revert" of the verse before it. Read it as the answer to that promise and the verse says: if they were sent back and reached the world, they would say the very thing they are saying now. **"There is nothing beyond this worldly life"** is the claim that this life, and nothing else, is real. **"and we will never be resurrected"** denies being raised after death to give an account. The ones who say it here are the idolaters of Makkah, and their denial is not a doubt about what comes after, it is a settled refusal.

### How can a witness deny

A question sits on the surface of these verses. They have seen the return to life, the Day of Qiyamah, the reckoning, the taking of account, the reward and the punishment. Once a person has seen all that, how can he go back to denying it? The answer is that denial does not require real uncertainty. A person can be certain and still deny. Look at the unbelievers and wrongdoers of our own time: in spite of their knowledge of Islamic realities they keep to denial and falsification, simply out of hostility. The Qur'an describes precisely that temper in the words about people who kept denying the signs while their own hearts were sure of them, and did it only out of wrongdoing and pride (27:14). Musa put the same thing plainly to Firʿawn, whose people were not uncertain about the signs but unwilling to accept them: "Verily, you know that these signs have clearly been sent down by none but the Lord of the heavens and the earth as eye-opening evidence" (17:102). It is also what was said about some of the People of the Book, who recognized the Last Prophet ﷺ the way they recognized their own sons and remained bent on opposing him.

So to sum up: the Creator knows with His eternal knowledge that their claim, that they would become ideal believers if only they were sent back, is a lie and a trick. If a world torn down were built up again and they were released into it, their conduct would be the conduct they had already shown in the lives they first lived.

### The scale and the offer

A reported saying of the Prophet ﷺ sets the same test at the center of the Day. At the time of the reckoning, Allah will ask Adam to stand near the Scale of Justice, to look at the deeds of his children, and to let into Paradise anyone whose good deeds outweigh his sins. Then He will say: the one I admit to the punishment of Hell is the one about whom I know that, if he were sent back into the world, he would do the same thing he had been doing. The verdict rests not on what a person promises under pressure but on what he would actually do.

### In short

- The verse quotes the creed behind all the rest: nothing beyond this life, and no resurrection.
- It continues verse 28, since reverting means saying this same thing again in the world.
- Denial can coexist with certainty, as 27:14 shows about those who rejected the signs out of pride.
- Allah's eternal knowledge already knows that their promise would not be kept.
- The saying about Adam and the Scale makes the sentence about what a person would really do again.

30.text:
"But if only you could see when they will be detained before their Lord!" The address now repeats the opening of verse 27 and moves the scene one step further. There they were stopped before the Fire. Here they are brought before their Lord, held there, constrained, and questioned, and the questioning is the kind that convicts rather than informs.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But if only you could see"** is again said to Muhammad ﷺ, and again its answer is left to be understood: you would certainly see an awesome thing. **"when they will be detained before their Lord"** means being set before Him and hemmed in, with no way to step aside from the address. **"He will ask ˹them˺, 'Is this ˹Hereafter˺ not the truth?'"** is a rebuke, not a request for news. The sense is: is not this resurrection and reckoning real, the torment and the rising after death, contrary to what you reckoned? One reading takes the question as coming from Allah to them, and another explains it as the angels asking it in rebuke on His tongue. **"They will cry, 'Absolutely, by our Lord!'"** is an oath by the Lord who created them: it is the truth, and there is no doubt about it, exactly as the messengers reported it. **"He will say, 'Then taste the punishment for your disbelief'"** is the sentence, and its point is that the retribution is the result of their denial of this day, which they went on rejecting through the whole of the life of the world.

### Why the admission arrives too late

The confession is honest, and worthless. On this Day they will affirm with an oath what they had denied in the world, because nothing is left but affirming it. Belief that arrives when the unseen has become seen does not count, and the verse before this one had already shown why their acceptance cannot be trusted: it is produced by what is in front of them, not by conviction. That is the same rule that made their wish to be sent back a lie. A thing believed only when it cannot be escaped is not believed in the way that was asked of them.

### A question asked in rebuke

Other verses put the same rebuke in other words, and one of them sharpens it: "Is this magic, or do you not see?" (52:15). The questioners know the answer before they ask. The point of asking is to make the denyers say it out loud in front of everyone, so that the sentence falls on a mouth that has just admitted the truth. Their Lord asks whether it is real, they swear that it is, and the punishment is then named as theirs by their own account, because it is the punishment for disbelief, not for bad luck.

### In short

- The scene of 6:27 is repeated at a higher place: before the Fire, and then before their Lord.
- "Is this not the truth?" is a rebuke about resurrection, the reckoning and the torment, not a question seeking information.
- Their answer is an oath that it is the truth, exactly as the messengers said.
- The sentence "taste the punishment for your disbelief" ties the torment to their denial of this day in the world.
- Admitting the truth when it can no longer be escaped does not change the verdict.

31.text:
"Losers indeed are those who deny the meeting with Allah until the Hour takes them by surprise." The verse names the loss before it describes the scene, and the scene is the moment the loss is discovered. These are people who denied the encounter with Allah through resurrection, who thought it farfetched, and who went on living as if nothing were owed. Then the Hour arrives without notice, and the death that begins it is part of what they refused to expect.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Losers indeed are those who deny the meeting with Allah"** speaks of a loss that is total, not a bad bargain. The denial is not of a story but of an encounter, their own meeting with Allah after death. **"until the Hour takes them by surprise"** marks the end of the delay they counted on, and the wording is there to expose how far their claim reached: nothing announces the Hour to them first. **"then they will cry, 'Woe to us for having ignored this'"** is regret in its purest form. The cry is an appeal to grief itself, as if to say: now is the time for you, grief, come out. What they mourn is not a sin they committed but an attention they never gave, faith and repentance left undone in the world. **"They will bear ˹the burden of˺ their sins on their backs"** is their load, and **"Evil indeed is their burden"** is the verdict on it.

### What the load looks like

The phrase in verse 31 about carrying their burdens is explained by narrations about the Day of Qiyamah, in which the deeds of good people become the mount they ride and the evil deeds of evil people are laid on them like a weight. A saying preserved from As-Suddi tells what happens at the threshold of the grave. Every unjust person is met, on entering it, by a man with an ugly face, dark skin, a foul smell and dirty clothes, who goes in with him. The unjust man asks how ugly that face is, and the answer comes: your own work was as ugly as this. He asks about the stench, and is told his work stunk. He asks about the filthy clothes, and is told his work was filthy. Then he asks who the stranger is, and the reply is: I am your deeds. That companion stays with him in the grave. When he is raised on the Day of Resurrection, the companion says: in the world I carried you, because you followed desire and lust, and today you carry me. So he climbs onto the unjust man's back and rides him until they both enter the Fire. This is how the burdens are borne, and this is why they are called evil. On the Day itself they come to them in the vilest forms and with the most putrid smells, and they are made to ride them.

### Why belief has to be about the unseen

These people will try anything on that Day to save themselves. They are nervous and confused. Sometimes they take refuge in a false oath, sometimes they beg to be returned to the world they had. What none of them ever says is: now we have believed, and now we will do nothing but good. The reason is that the hereafter is not the place of deeds. Once a person has seen, he is only agreeing with what is in front of him. That is not what a declaration of belief in Allah and His Messenger was ever meant to be. The hereafter is not the Dar al-Amal, the place where deeds are done. Sound iman depends on being about the ghayb, the unseen, with no need to see. And the other side of that is the terrible usefulness of this present life. Working for the pleasure of Allah, earning the promised everlasting bliss, hoping for Paradise and for a quiet good life right now: all of it can happen only in this world, neither before it nor after it. It cannot be done in the universe of spirits beforehand, and it cannot be done once the world of our experience is gone. That is why this life is a great blessing and an asset nothing else matches, and why harming oneself is forbidden, and praying for death, and even wishing for it, since all of that is ingratitude for a blessing.

### In short

- The verse states the loss first, then the surprise: people who denied the meeting with Allah are overtaken by the Hour.
- Their cry is regret for neglect, an appeal to grief itself, and a wish for the faith and repentance they left undone.
- The burden on their backs is their own deeds, described as a companion at the grave who turns the riding around on the Day of Rising.
- Acceptance after seeing does not count, because faith is meant to be about the unseen.
- This world is the only place where any of it can be earned, which is why it is a blessing and not to be thrown away.

32.text:
"This worldly life is no more than play and amusement, but far better is the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter for those mindful ˹of Allah˺." The two halves are set side by side on purpose. On one side is what is passing, on the other what is better. The choice between them is made with the mind.

### Phrase by phrase

**"This worldly life is no more than play and amusement"** is about the part of a life spent being heedless of Allah. The sense is that most of it is that, a pastime and a worthless activity. **"but far better is the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter"** means Paradise. It is better for the people who keep their duty, who ward off disbelief, association and indecency. **"for those mindful ˹of Allah˺"** ties the better home to taqwa. Taqwa is a life built on the assumption that the world belongs to Allah. **"Will you not then understand"** is the question that closes the verse. One reading takes it as addressed to the idolaters: do you not understand this, so that you believe and do good actions.

### What is actually censured

The condemnation of worldly life here, in other verses and in many hadiths, is not a condemnation of wealth or of the world itself. It is aimed at the time of life spent heedless of Allah. Set against that, nothing in this world is worth what one hour of dhikr is worth, of remembering Him and doing what He commanded. A hadith puts the same line very sharply: the world and everything in it lies under a ban, except the remembrance of Allah, a knowledgeable person and a student. The teacher of religion and the student of religion belong under that exception. The knowledge in question is knowledge that earns the pleasure of Allah. Imam al-Jazri drew the circle wider still. Whatever is done in this world in obedience to Allah, inside the limits of the Shari'ah, counts as remembrance of Him. On that reading, everything that has to be done to hold a life together is included, and so is every permissible way of earning a living. The rights of family, relatives, neighbours, friends and guests have been named as sadaqah, and as worship.

So the dearest thing a person owns is his time. That time is limited, and nobody knows how long it is. It may be seventy years. It may be seventy hours. It may be no more than the span of one breath. Everything in this world that is worth Allah's favour comes down to obedience and remembrance. A hadith of the Prophet ﷺ gives the arithmetic. The wise man is the one who takes hold of himself, is content with little, and sends his deeds ahead to what comes after death.

### A question with two readings

The closing question begins with a-fa-lā, and the verb qilūna at its end is read two ways, and both readings are kept. With a ta it is put to the listeners, with a ya it asks about them. A second point of the same kind sits in the middle of the verse, where the Home of the Hereafter can be read as one phrase or split into two. Either way the question does the same work. Do you not understand that this world is passing and the hereafter lasting, and will you not believe?

### In short

- The verse weighs a passing life of heedlessness against a lasting home, and calls the second one better.
- Play and amusement means the time spent careless of Allah, not the world as such.
- Whatever is done in obedience to Allah inside the limits of the Shari'ah falls under remembrance. The rights of family and neighbours fall under worship.
- Life is short and its length is unknown, which is why the hadith names self-control, contentment and deeds sent ahead as wisdom.
- The closing question is left open on purpose, and its two readings make the address either about them or to you.

33.text:
"We certainly know that what they say grieves you ˹O Prophet˺." The verse is a comfort before it is anything else. Allah tells His messenger that the grief is known to Him, that the sorrow he carries over his people has not escaped notice, and then it re-labels what the grief is really about.

### Phrase by phrase

**"what they say grieves you"** covers their denial of him, their slander and their demands for proofs. Other verses say the same thing in harder words: "So destroy not yourself in sorrow for them" (35:8), "It may be that you are going to kill yourself with grief, that they do not become believers" (26:3), and "Perhaps you would kill yourself in grief over their footsteps, because they believe not in this narration" (18:6). **"It is not your honesty they question"** means they do not accuse him of lying. They knew him too well for that. A variant reading takes the words as a statement rather than a denial, and renders it: they do not charge you with mendacity. **"it is Allah's signs that the wrongdoers deny"** turns the rejection back onto its real object. What they refuse is the truth itself and the signs of Allah, and the denial is carried out openly while it is refused inwardly. On another reading they do reject the Prophet outwardly, but the outcome of belying him is the belying of Allah and His signs, and a hadith puts the same equation the other way round: whoever causes pain to the Prophet causes pain to Allah.

### What three chiefs did at night

Muhammad ibn Isḥāq related from az-Zuhrī that three men came to listen to the Prophet ﷺ reciting the Qur'an at night, each of them unaware of the others: Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, Ṣakhr ibn Ḥarb who is Abū Sufyān, and al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq. They stayed until morning and left, met on the way back, were asked by one another what had brought them, told the truth, and swore not to repeat it, so that the young men of Quraysh would not hear of it and imitate them. On the second night every one of them came back, each assuming the others would keep away because of the oath. They met again in the morning, blamed one another and swore again, and on the third night they did the same thing for the third time.

Then al-Akhnas took his staff and went to Abū Sufyān at his house and said: "O Abū Ḥanzalah, what is your view of what you heard from Muḥammad?" He answered: "O Abu Tha'labah, by Allah, I heard things I recognized and knew the reach of, and things whose meaning was closed to me." Al-Akhnas said the same of himself, by Him whom the other had sworn by, and went on to Abū Jahl, whom he addressed as "O Abū al-Ḥakam". Abū Jahl said: we raced with Banū ʿAbd Manāf and matched them. We fed as they fed and gave as they gave, and when we were neck and neck with them, like two horses in a race, they said: there is a prophet among us, and revelation comes down to him from heaven. How could we catch them up on that? By Allah, believing in him and accepting what he says is something we will never do. In Arabia he had been called Abū al-Ḥakam, a man of wisdom, and was renamed for his hostility.

A second account, preserved through As-Suddi, lays the same scene out more briefly. Akhnas ibn Shurayq met Abū Jahl and said: you and I are alone, no third person is listening, so tell me what you really think of Muḥammad ibn ʿAbdullāh, is he telling the truth or not. Abū Jahl answered that Muḥammad is truthful, with no doubt about it, and that he has never told a lie in his life. But we cannot bear that one branch of Quraysh, Banū Quṣayy, should hold every virtue while the rest of the tribe has nothing. They have the banner.
